title: Identify Excessive or Duplicative Research Charges in Litigation Invoice

blind.coverage: I read all six supplied documents in full: the July invoice (all 160 fee-detail rows, the disbursements, the discount sheet and the summary), the billing guidelines, the engagement letter, the June invoice summary, Holt's June 28 email and the DOE-matter invoice. I also read all 46 criteria and the instructions. I recomputed the invoice arithmetic with a script: the fee-detail total, research totals by timekeeper, the discount and the percentages. I read the grading prompts only as described in the task and did not open them. No external legal authority was needed, because every criterion turns on the client's own billing guidelines, a contract document, not on statute or case law. I cite no outside authorities. Not verified: whether the $106K gap between the fee detail and the stated fees is an artifact of how the task was built (for example, detail that was left out on purpose). Either way the supplied record is what the solver and the judges see.

findings.title: Itemized fee entries total $243,080.50, not the invoice's stated $349,552.50 gross; rubric percentages assume the unsupported total
findings.explanation: The 160 Fee Detail rows (every rate × hours checks out) sum to $243,080.50 across 565.9 hours. The Summary claims gross fees of $349,552.50, which leaves $106,472 in fees with no time entries behind them. Research hours also conflict: 142.3 on the Summary versus 137.6 on the Discount sheet and in the detail. C-002, C-003 and C-006 hard-code 13.56%, 15.83% and $41,018, all computed on the unsupported $341,820.50 net figure. A careful reviewer who recomputes from the entries gets research at about 19.7% net (22.3% gross) and a cap of about $28,242. If the memo reports only those figures, it fails three criteria even though it is more accurate. The rubric also never credits the unsupported $106K, which is arguably the largest non-compliant charge under an instruction to find 'all non-compliant or excessive charges.' C-036 calls $387,420.50 the 'correct' total, though the line items do not support it.

evidence.quote: A19='Total Professional Fees (Gross):' | B19='$349,552.50'
A28='Total Research Hours:' | B28='142.3'
A15='Total Research Hours:' | B15='137.6'
net research charges ($46,372.50) as a percentage of total fees ($341,820.50) is approximately 13.5%-13.6%

findings.suggested_fix: Fix the invoice so the detail rows sum to the stated gross fees. Otherwise, let C-002, C-003 and C-006 accept figures computed on either the stated or the itemized fees, and add credit for flagging the unsupported fees.

findings.title: C-025 misstates Section 6.5: no '50% must be non-research' requirement and no 'research cap rate' exists
findings.explanation: Section 6.5 requires that block-billed research entries clearly allocate time. If research is more than 50% of the entry, or the allocation is unclear, the whole entry is treated as Legal Research and counts in full toward the 6.2 cap. If non-research time is 50% or more and clearly stated, only the research portion counts. Nothing requires firms to put 50% of the time on non-research work, and nothing reduces an entry to a 'research cap rate'; no such rate exists, and the rate schedule expressly says there is no separate research rate. C-025 takes its wording from Holt's paraphrase in his email, not from the guideline. A memo that accurately says 'an unallocated or research-predominant entry counts in full toward the cap' does not say what C-025 requires and may be failed. A memo that repeats the incorrect paraphrase is rewarded.

evidence.quote: If the research component constitutes more than fifty percent (50%) of the block-billed entry's total time, or if the allocation between research and non-research tasks is unclear from the description, the entire entry will be treated as a Legal Research entry and will count in full toward the Research Cap
must allocate at least 50% of the time to the non-research component, or the entire entry will be reduced to the research cap rate
No alternative or reduced rates (including any separate "research rate") are established under this schedule

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo explains the 6.5 allocation rule and its 50% threshold: research-predominant or unallocated entries count in full toward the 12% cap. Delete the 'research cap rate' language.

findings.title: Severity ratings are required but never requested
findings.explanation: The instructions ask for a memo that identifies non-compliant or excessive charges with recommended adjustments. Severity or priority ratings are not a standard part of an invoice-review memo; the dollar adjustment already conveys magnitude. A memo that lists every violation with its guideline citation and dollar adjustment, without labels like Critical or Minor, fails C-038 and therefore scores zero on the all-pass metric.

evidence.quote: prepare a memo identifying all non-compliant or excessive charges with recommended adjustments
FAIL if no severity assessments or priority rankings are provided.

findings.suggested_fix: Delete C-038, or make it non-gating.

findings.title: C-003 requires a pre-discount research percentage the guideline does not use, with a mixed denominator
findings.explanation: Section 6.2 defines research charges as measured after any voluntary discounts, so the governing figure is the net 13.56% (C-002). C-003 also requires 'gross research ÷ net fees' of 15.8–15.9%, a mixed-basis ratio no instruction or guideline calls for. A memo that correctly applies 6.2 and reports only the net figure fails. A memo that computes the natural pre-discount comparison, gross research over gross fees (54,104.50 / 349,552.50 = 15.48%), falls outside the 15.8–15.9% band and also risks failing.

evidence.quote: "total Legal Research charges" means ... after application of any voluntary discounts or write-downs by outside counsel
approximately 15.8%-15.9% (the exact figure is 15.83%). FAIL if the gross percentage is not calculated.

findings.suggested_fix: Delete C-003, or make it optional credit that accepts any clearly labeled pre-discount ratio.

findings.title: Block-billing criterion demands three Osei entries that are research-memo work already coded RES, while better examples are excluded
findings.explanation: Under the Section 2 definition, drafting a research memorandum that compiles research findings is itself Legal Research. The three required entries (Osei July 3, 8 and 16) are therefore arguably not 'research + non-research' block billing. All three are also already coded RES and counted in full toward the cap, so 6.5 changes nothing for them. The clearest 6.5 problem is Osei's July 11 entry, coded DRF ('Assist with drafting meet-and-confer letter; research local rules'), whose research component escapes the cap; Wendt's July 11 RES entry ('Research and prepare opposition arguments') is another. A memo that flags those, correctly, under 6.5 fails C-024.

evidence.quote: preparing research summaries or memoranda to the extent such memoranda primarily compile or synthesize research findings
H122='DRF' | I122='Assist with drafting meet-and-confer letter; research local rules on meet-and-confer requirements for discovery motions.'
references at least one of: Amara Osei July 3 ... Osei July 8 ... or Osei July 16

findings.suggested_fix: Accept any entry that is plausibly block-billed research under 6.5, including Osei July 11 (DRF) and Wendt July 11.

findings.title: Section 4.3 by its terms covers only newly assigned timekeepers; Wendt and Osei have been staffed since January 2024
findings.explanation: Section 4.3 applies to 'a newly assigned Timekeeper'; its phrase list in (e) refers to educating 'the new Timekeeper'; and 6.4 speaks of 'new or rotating team members.' The engagement letter staffed Wendt and Osei from January 22, 2024, and both billed substantial time in June. The 'get up to speed' and 'familiarize' entries are clearly objectionable, but a careful reviewer may say 4.3 applies only by analogy and rest the disallowance on 4.1, 6.1, or the reasonableness reservation in Sections 11–12. C-021 and C-041 treat 4.3 as plainly the provision violated. A precise memo that hedges on 4.3, or cites other sections, risks failing.

evidence.quote: Time spent by a newly assigned Timekeeper reviewing the existing file, getting up to speed on the Matter, performing background research ... is not billable
Tyler Wendt            Associate (4th year)          Motion practice and legal research
FAIL if Section 4.3 is not cited in connection with these entries.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the entries are disallowed as familiarization or background research under 4.3 (directly or by analogy), 6.4, 4.1, or the reasonableness provisions.

findings.title: C-019's model remedy disallows the junior attorney's time, contrary to Section 6.4's pay-the-junior rule
findings.explanation: Section 6.4 says that when research overlaps, TerraVerde pays the most junior qualified attorney and disallows higher-rate timekeepers. For the July 12 economic loss rule entries, that means paying Osei ($295) and disallowing Takahashi (6.0 hrs × $340 = $2,040). C-019 instead names Osei's $1,327.50 as the minimum disallowance. Its lenient wording ('or a comparable amount'; FAIL only if no adjustment) probably still passes a correct $2,040 disallowance. But it signals the wrong remedy, and a judge could read 'comparable' narrowly. Osei also covered the economic loss rule earlier, on July 10.

evidence.quote: TerraVerde will pay for the time of the most junior qualified attorney who performed the research, and charges for higher-rate Timekeepers performing overlapping research will be disallowed.
At minimum, Osei's 4.5 hours at $295/hr = $1,327.50 should be recommended for disallowance or a comparable amount.

findings.suggested_fix: Name Takahashi's $2,040 as the 6.4-consistent adjustment, and accept any reasonable dollar adjustment.

findings.title: Damages-duplication criterion requires the 'lost profits is a subset' framing and skips Takahashi's July 3 consequential-damages entry
findings.explanation: The clearest damages duplications in the record are two pairs. Takahashi on July 3 ('consequential damages in breach of remediation contracts') overlaps Osei on July 8 and 10. Wendt and Takahashi both researched lost profits on the same day, July 18. C-016 requires the memo to link Osei's consequential-damages work to the July 18 lost-profits entries and to say lost profits is a subset. A memo that flags both duplications as separate pairs, without the subset language, could be failed even though it identifies more duplication than the criterion lists.

evidence.quote: I12='Research Washington law on consequential damages in breach of remediation contracts; survey damages limitations.'
noting that lost profits is a subset of consequential damages

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo identifies duplicative damages research across any of these timekeepers; make the subset framing optional.

findings.title: Record conflicts on reply-brief filing date and on the timing and content of Holt's review of the June invoice
findings.explanation: The July invoice records the reply brief as filed twice. On July 11 Vogel's entry reads 'file with court' and Hargrove's reads 'approve for filing'; on July 19 there are fresh 'final review', 'authorize filing' and 'E-file' entries. Briggs then billed research 'for reply brief' on July 15. C-034 assumes a single July 19 filing. Holt's email, dated June 28, says he 'completed my review of the... June 2024 invoices' and that June research was 'approaching or pushing against' the 12% cap. But the June invoice is dated July 8 and reports research at 4.13%. None of this is likely to fail a memo outright, but these inconsistencies bear on how incremental the July work was, and a reviewer who notices them has no clear answer.

evidence.quote: I37='Prepare reply brief for e-filing; verify formatting compliance with W.D. Wash. local rules; file with court.'
I64='E-file reply brief and supporting exhibits with W.D. Wash.; serve on opposing counsel via CM/ECF.'
June 2024 research charges represent 4.13% of total professional fees
the June 2024 invoice shows research charges approaching or pushing against the 12% cap

findings.suggested_fix: Make the reply-brief entries show a single filing date and make the email consistent with the June invoice (date and research percentage). Otherwise, credit memos that flag the duplicate filing entries.

findings.title: C-028 overstates the cross-matter overlap: only about 7.5 of Takahashi's 12.5 DOE research hours match the Cascade research
findings.explanation: Takahashi's DOE entries on July 1, 2 and 8 (7.5 hrs) match his Cascade MTCA and CERCLA research. The July 15 entry ('DOE enforcement precedent and prior consent decrees') and the July 22 entry ('DOE enforcement procedures... defenses to DOE enforcement actions') are specific to the DOE proceeding. C-028 says the Cascade research 'overlaps substantially with 12.5 hours.' A memo that quantifies the overlap more carefully (5.5–7.5 hrs) may still pass, but a strict judge could read the 12.5-hour figure as required.

evidence.quote: "Research Washington DOE enforcement procedures under MTCA; analyze remediation contractor defenses to DOE enforcement actions and relationship to private party claims."
overlaps substantially with 12.5 hours of MTCA research he billed to the separate DOE Matter

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo identifies overlap between Takahashi's Cascade MTCA research and his DOE-billed MTCA research under 6.6, whatever overlap figure it gives.

blind.overall: The rubric correctly spots the main planted issues: the 12% cap exceedance, partner research at partner rates, the Westlaw pass-through, the discount arithmetic, cross-matter and same-month duplication, and the database-hosting distractor. Most criteria match the guideline text, and the 6.3 and 6.4 remedies are mostly right. The biggest defect is in the supplied invoice. The itemized entries total $243,080.50, but the summary claims $349,552.50 gross, so the hard-coded 13.56%, 15.83% and $41,018 figures rest on $106K of fees with no time entries behind them, and a reviewer who works from the line items can fail several criteria. C-025 misstates Section 6.5, C-038 requires severity ratings no one asked for, and C-003 requires a gross ratio the guideline does not use. Each can zero out a competent memo under all-pass grading. Several more criteria (the Section 4.3 scope, the block-billing examples, the damages-subset framing, the economic-loss remedy) are defensible but brittle for careful answers.

sol_verdicts.reason: Section 6.5 has no rule that at least 50% of an entry must be non-research, and it has no 'research cap rate'. Research-predominant or unclearly allocated entries count in full toward the 12% cap. The engagement letter expressly says there is no separate research rate. C-025 takes its wording from Holt's inaccurate paraphrase, so it rewards the misstatement and can fail a memo that states the rule correctly.

I independently confirmed the gap: the 160 detail rows sum to $243,080.50, against $349,552.50 stated on the Summary. C-002, C-003 and C-006 hard-code percentages and a cap figure that rest on $106K of fees with no supporting entries, so a reconciling memo can fail. C-036 only asks the memo to state the invoice total. Quoting the billed total while noting the gap would still pass, so C-036 is merely arguable.

Osei's July 10 entry also covers the economic loss rule, and July 8 includes memo drafting, so '13 hours on one question' overstates it. But research-memo drafting falls within the Section 2 research definition, and flagging 13 hours as disproportionate under 6.1 is a reasonable position. The problem is that the rubric demands one judgment call, which is debatable rather than clearly wrong. I see no real conflict with C-024, because 6.5 treats unallocated entries as research.

Section 4.3 covers a 'newly assigned Timekeeper', and Wendt has been staffed since January 2024. The July 15 entry ('familiarize with MTCA amendments and recent regulatory guidance') could be substantive update research. A memo that queries or conditionally holds that entry, or rests its objection on 6.4, 6.1 or the reasonableness reservation instead of 4.3, risks failing C-022, C-023 or C-041. I exclude C-021, because the July 25 entry literally uses the 4.3(e) phrases 'review file materials' and 'get up to speed'.

Section 6.4 puts the burden on outside counsel to show that apparently duplicative entries addressed genuinely distinct questions. The client's reviewer is right to flag these overlaps, and most of these criteria accept 'any reasonable adjustment'. The DOE summary itself says both matters center on MTCA contractor strict liability. Only C-016 (required subset framing), C-017 (an excess judgment call) and C-019 (a model remedy contrary to 6.4) are arguable.

Neither the instructions nor Holt's email asks for severity or priority ratings, and they are not a standard part of an invoice-adjustment memo, where dollar adjustments already show magnitude. C-038 fails any memo without rankings. Under all-pass grading, that zeroes out a complete, correct memo, so I rate it problematic rather than arguable.

final.changes_from_blind:
1. I split C-036 out of blind O1 into its own arguable finding (O5). Stating the billed total while flagging the gap would still pass C-036, so it is less brittle than C-002, C-003 and C-006.
2. From Sol, I adopted C-017 as arguable (O8), not problematic. The July 10 entry does add economic-loss-rule work, but calling the hours excessive is a defensible 6.1 judgment.
3. I narrowed blind O6 to C-022, C-023 and C-041, following Sol's point that the July 15 update research may be substantive. I dropped C-021, whose entry uses the 4.3(e) phrases verbatim, and C-046, which expressly accepts other provisions or 'excessive'.
4. I dropped blind O10 (C-028). The DOE summary says both matters center on MTCA contractor strict liability, and the July 15 and July 22 DOE entries continue that research. The 12.5-hour DOE total is a fair characterization, and the PASS condition requires only identifying the cross-matter duplication.
5. I dropped blind O9 (C-005, C-033, C-034). The inconsistencies in the reply-brief filing dates and the June email are real, but they do not change what a correct answer is or cause any criterion to misgrade.
6. I rejected Sol's broad arguable/1 cluster except for C-016, C-017 and C-019. Section 6.4 shifts the burden to outside counsel, so flagging the MTCA, economic-loss, spoliation and unjust-enrichment overlaps is right, and the adjustment criteria accept any reasonable amount.
7. I kept C-038 as problematic, which is more severe than Sol's rating.
final.overall: The rubric correctly targets the main planted issues: the 12% cap exceedance, partner research at partner rates, the Westlaw pass-through, the discount arithmetic, within-matter and cross-matter duplication, and the database-hosting distractor. Most of the duplication criteria are sound, because 6.4 puts the burden on counsel. The largest defect is in the record: the itemized fees ($243,080.50) do not support the stated $349,552.50 gross, so the hard-coded 13.56%, 15.83% and $41,018 figures (C-002, C-003, C-006) rest on $106K of fees with no time entries behind them. C-025 misstates Section 6.5 by copying Holt's paraphrase. C-038 (severity ratings) and C-003 (a mixed-basis gross ratio) require unrequested content that can zero out a competent memo under all-pass grading. The Section 4.3 onboarding criteria, the block-billing examples, the damages-subset framing, Osei's 'excessive' hours, the economic-loss remedy and the C-036 total are defensible but brittle for careful answers.
final.coverage: I reviewed all 46 criteria and the instructions. In the blind pass I read all six documents in full and recomputed the invoice arithmetic. In this pass I re-checked every RES entry, the guideline text of 4.3, 6.1, 6.4 and 6.6, and the DOE-matter research entries against each Sol finding. I read Sol's full markdown and JSON audit. No external legal authority was needed, because every criterion turns on the client's billing guidelines, a contract document, and I cite none.
